In [[probability theory]], '''lumpability''' is a method for reducing the size of the state space of some [[continuous-time Markov chain]]s, first published by [[John George Kemeny|Kemeny]] and [[J. Laurie Snell|Snell]].<ref>
{{cite book

==Definition==
Suppose that the complete state-space of a [[Markov chain]] is divided into disjoint subsets of states, where these subsets are denoted by ''t<sub>i</sub>''. This forms  a [[partition of a set|partition]] <math>\scriptstyle{T = \{ t_1, t_2, \ldots \}}</math> of the states. Both the state-space and the collection of subsets may be either finite or countably infinite.
A continuous-time Markov chain <math>\{ X_i \}</math> is '''lumpable''' with respect to the partition ''T'' if and only if, for any subsets ''t<sub>i</sub>'' and ''t<sub>j</sub>'' in the partition, and for any states ''n,n’'' in subset ''t<sub>i</sub>'',

: <math>\sum_{m \in t_j} q(n,m) = \sum_{m \in t_j} q(n',m) ,</math>

where ''q''(''i,j'') is the transition rate from state ''i'' to state ''j''.<ref>[[Jane Hillston]], [http://www.dcs.ed.ac.uk/pepa/compositional.ps.gz ''Compositional Markovian Modelling Using A Process Algebra''] in the Proceedings of the Second International Workshop on Numerical Solution of Markov Chains: Computations with Markov Chains, Raleigh, North Carolina, January 1995. Kluwer Academic Press</ref> 

Similarly, for a [[stochastic matrix]] ''P'', ''P'' is a '''lumpable matrix''' on a partition ''T'' if and only if, for any subsets ''t<sub>i</sub>'' and ''t<sub>j</sub>'' in the partition, and for any states ''n,n’'' in subset ''t<sub>i</sub>'',

: <math>\sum_{m \in t_j} p(n,m) = \sum_{m \in t_j} p(n',m) ,</math>

where ''p''(''i,j'') is the probability of moving from state ''i'' to state ''j''.<ref>[[Peter Harrison (computer scientist)|Peter G. Harrison]] and Naresh M. Patel, ''Performance Modelling of Communication Networks and Computer Architectures'' Addison-Wesley 1992</ref>

==Example==

Consider the matrix

: <math>P = \begin{pmatrix}
\frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{8} & \frac{1}{16} & \frac{1}{16} \\
\frac{7}{16} & \frac{7}{16} & 0 & \frac{1}{8} \\
\frac{1}{16} & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{7}{16} \\
0 & \frac{1}{16} & \frac{3}{8} & \frac{9}{16} \end{pmatrix}</math>

and notice it is lumpable on the partition ''t''&nbsp;=&nbsp;{(1,2),(3,4)} so we write

: <math>P_t = \begin{pmatrix}
\frac{7}{8} & \frac{1}{8} \\
\frac{1}{16} & \frac{15}{16} \end{pmatrix}</math>

and call ''P''<sub>''t''</sub> the lumped matrix of ''P'' on ''t''.

== Successively lumpable processes ==

In 2012, [[Michael N. Katehakis|Katehakis]] and Smit discovered the Successively Lumpable processes for which the stationary probabilities can be obtained by successively computing the stationary probabilities of a propitiously constructed sequence of Markov chains. Each of the latter chains has a (typically much) smaller state space and this yields significant computational improvements.  These results have many applications reliability and queueing models and problems.<ref name="mnksmit">{{Cite journal | last1 = Katehakis | first1 = M. N. | author-link1 = Michael Katehakis| last2 = Smit | first2 = L. C. | doi = 10.1017/S0269964812000150 | title = A Successive Lumping Procedure for a Class of Markov Chains | journal = Probability in the Engineering and Informational Sciences | volume = 26 | issue = 4 | pages = 483 | year = 2012 }}</ref>

==Quasi–lumpability==

Franceschinis and Muntz introduced quasi-lumpability, a property whereby a small change in the rate matrix makes the chain lumpable.<ref name="fra">{{cite journal |last1=Franceschinis |first1=G. |last2=Muntz |first2=Richard R. |year=1993 |title=Bounds for quasi-lumpable Markov chains |journal=[[Performance Evaluation]] |publisher=Elsevier B.V. |volume=20 |issue=1–3 |pages=223–243 |doi=10.1016/0166-5316(94)90015-9}}</ref>
